1917 - The Balfour Declaration

Britain declared its support for the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people. The territory subsequently covered by the Mandate for Palestine included the lands of present-day Israel and Jordan, as well as the West Bank and Gaza.

In 1920, the Allied powers met in San Remo, Italy, and agreed to incorporate that commitment into the British Mandate for Palestine. In 1922, the League of Nations formally approved the mandate, explicitly recognizing the Jewish people’s historical connection to the land.

This recognition did not create that connection. It acknowledged it.

Even the Hashemite leadership acknowledged the Jewish people’s ancestral connection to the land while still ruling Islam’s holy cities in Arabia.

On March 23, 1918, Al-Qibla, the official newspaper of Hussein bin Ali, King of the Hejaz and Sharif of Mecca, published an article recognizing that connection. Hussein was a leading figure in the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans, supported by Britain.

The article described Palestine as “a sacred and beloved homeland” for the Jews, referring to them as “its original sons.” It also spoke positively about the return of Jewish exiles to their homeland and the benefits their work could bring to the region.

These words appeared in the official newspaper of a Hashemite ruler more than thirty years before the establishment of the modern State of Israel.

But Britain’s policies increasingly departed from the hopes raised by its commitment. In 1921, Britain established an administration in Transjordan under the Hashemite Emir Abdullah. In 1922, with League approval, the provisions concerning the Jewish national home were excluded from the territory east of the Jordan River - roughly three-quarters of the territory covered by the mandate.

Transjordan later became an independent kingdom in 1946.
